title: Practise Now 3(2)
summary: Find HI in ΔGIH, then IR = HI − RH, then GR in ΔGIR.
alt: Practise Now 3(2): In ΔGHI, GH = 61 cm, GI = 11 cm and ∠I = 90°. R lies on IH such that RH = 21 cm. Find the length of (i) HI, (ii) GR.

hyp.label: Hypotenuse
hyp.text: The side opposite the right angle. It is always the longest side.

legA.label: Shorter side 1
legA.text: One of the two sides that meet at the right angle.

legB.label: Shorter side 2
legB.text: The other side that meets at the right angle.

steps.title: The question
steps.narration: In **ΔGHI**, **GH = 61 cm**, **GI = 11 cm** and **∠I = 90°**. **R** lies on **IH** such that **RH = 21 cm**. We have to find (i) **HI** and (ii) **GR**. (The figure is not drawn to scale.)

steps.title: Spot the right angle
steps.narration: In ΔGIH, **∠I = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **GH**. The other two sides meet at the right angle.

steps.title: Pythagoras' theorem
steps.narration: **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{GH^2} &= \role{legA}{GI^2} + \role{legB}{HI^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Make the unknown the subject
steps.narration: We want a **shorter side**, so subtract the known square from the hypotenuse square.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{GH^2} &= \role{legA}{GI^2} + \role{legB}{HI^2} \\ \role{legB}{HI^2} &= \role{hyp}{GH^2} - \role{legA}{GI^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute the lengths
steps.narration: Replace each side by its length.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{GH^2} &= \role{legA}{GI^2} + \role{legB}{HI^2} \\ \role{legB}{HI^2} &= \role{hyp}{GH^2} - \role{legA}{GI^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{61^2} - \role{legA}{11^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: Take the square root of both sides (a length is positive).\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{GH^2} &= \role{legA}{GI^2} + \role{legB}{HI^2} \\ \role{legB}{HI^2} &= \role{hyp}{GH^2} - \role{legA}{GI^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{61^2} - \role{legA}{11^2} \\ &= \role{hyp}{3721} - \role{legA}{121} \\ &= \role{legB}{3600} \\ \role{legB}{HI} &= \sqrt{3600} = \role{ans}{60\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Find IR
steps.narration: Now find the shorter part **IR**.\[\begin{aligned}IR &= HI - RH \\ &= 60 - 21 = 39\ \text{cm}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Right angle and theorem
steps.narration: In ΔGIR, **∠I = 90°**, so the **hypotenuse** is the side opposite it: **GR**. The other two sides meet at the right angle. **Pythagoras' theorem**: the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{GR^2} &= \role{legA}{GI^2} + \role{legB}{IR^2}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Substitute and add
steps.narration: Put in the lengths, square them and add.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{GR^2} &= \role{legA}{GI^2} + \role{legB}{IR^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{11^2} + \role{legB}{39^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{121} + \role{legB}{1521} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1642}\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Square root
steps.narration: 1642 is not a perfect square, so use a calculator and round to 3 significant figures.\[\begin{aligned}\role{hyp}{GR^2} &= \role{legA}{GI^2} + \role{legB}{IR^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{11^2} + \role{legB}{39^2} \\ &= \role{legA}{121} + \role{legB}{1521} \\ &= \role{hyp}{1642} \\ \role{hyp}{GR} &= \sqrt{1642} = \role{ans}{40.5\ \text{cm}}\end{aligned}\]

formulas.title: Pythagoras' theorem
formulas.text: In a right-angled triangle, the square on the hypotenuse equals the sum of the squares on the other two sides.

formulas.title: Finding the hypotenuse
formulas.text: Add the two squares, then take the square root.

formulas.title: Finding a shorter side
formulas.text: Subtract the known shorter side's square from the hypotenuse's square, then take the square root.

challenges.title: Check IR
challenges.prompt: HI = 60 cm and RH = 21 cm. How long is **IR**?

takeaways: Pythagoras' theorem works only in **right-angled** triangles — mark every right angle in the figure first.
Split the figure into right-angled triangles and solve them **one at a time**; each answer feeds the next triangle.
Keep a few extra decimal places in the middle of a calculation and round only the **final** answer (3 s.f.).

notes.title: Exam tip
notes.text: Always begin with a line such as "In ΔABC, ∠C = 90°. Using Pythagoras' Theorem," — it shows which triangle and which right angle you are using.

notes.title: Rounding
notes.text: If the answer is not a whole number, give it to **3 significant figures** unless the question says otherwise.
